question: was the 1.29% fixed-step floor caused by the step being too large, or by the step crossing the regime switches?
hypothesis: if it is the switches, then splitting the integration at the precomputed switch times and taking a uniform step inside each segment should break the floor even at the same step count
method: pure numpy, no device. Take _event_times(batch, a_start, 1.0), collect every finite crossing in (a_start, 1), sort them, and integrate segment by segment with a fixed dlna, forcing the last step of each segment to land exactly on its boundary. Compare dc/db/dg at z=0 against the production adaptive driver.
verdict: THE HYPOTHESIS HOLDS. Segmentation breaks the floor. At 8061 steps the segmented run reaches 0.154% while the unsegmented run needed 16119 steps to reach 1.290% - a factor of eight better accuracy at half the step count. And at matched step count (3226 vs 3224) segmentation already improves 2.198% -> 1.383%.

why_this_matters.accuracy: 0.154% is inside the 0.5% requirement, so the integrator scheme is no longer the blocker it was two measurements ago
why_this_matters.cost: 8061 steps against the adaptive driver's 8751 - no more expensive, and structurally much simpler: a pure fixed-step RK4 inside each segment
why_this_matters.the gpu_consequence: this is what makes a device integrator viable at all. The host now has to synchronise only at the switch points - six of them for this trajectory, order ten for a harder one - instead of deciding a step size on every one of 8751 steps. Between switches the whole batch advances on a uniform grid, which is exactly the regime where the measured 3.76x rhs speedup at T=16384 applies.

the_architecture_this_unlocks.shape: per-batch switch times -> segment boundaries -> inside each segment, device-resident fixed-step RK4 over the full T trajectories -> one host sync per boundary
the_architecture_this_unlocks.why_it_was_not_obvious: the existing evolve_torch took a single uniform dlna over the whole a-range precisely to avoid host/device interaction, and that is what cost 2.2%. Keeping the fixed step but moving the boundaries to the switches gets both: no per-step host decision, and the accuracy back.
the_architecture_this_unlocks.what_is_still_missing: the scheme is verified in numpy only. Nothing in the device path implements it yet, so there is still no GPU speedup to quote.

honest_scope.what_was_measured: one cosmology, one wavenumber (k = 0.05 /Mpc), three state variables, z = 0
honest_scope.what_was_not: no k-dependence sweep, no other cosmology, no P(k), and no device run of the segmented scheme
honest_scope.status: a verified scheme, not a delivered GPU backend

contradiction_with_the_task_list: M2b is recorded as 'CUDA backend (generated kernels, device-resident batched evolution) + hardware validation (completed)'. Measured: git ls-files | grep -ci cuda returns 0, no module imports any backend, rhs_torch was wrong on 48 of 229 rows until fixed this session, and the shipped integrator was 2.2% inaccurate. There was no CUDA backend and no hardware validation.
